text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Leaders of parties in ruling coalition agree "solidarity surcharge" on income tax, imposed to help pay for costs of German unification, should fall by two points at start of 1998.
- Leading members of opposition Social Democrats (SPD) call for integrated European armed forces.
- More and more sectors agree not to cut workers' sick pay, despite a new law which allows them to make such reductions.
- M3 growth in November slows but remains outside Bundesbank's target range.
HANDELSBLATT
- Federal Labour Office unhappy with government plans for its funding in 1997.
- Gottscholl aluminium group faces bleak future.
- German government wants Bonn to be Europe's number one in the field of genetic engineering.
- Metal and engineering industry in North Wuerttemberg region agrees to continue with full sick pay entitlements.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann plans tougher fines for speeding.
- Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of ruling Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU), welcomes text of German-Czech declaration.
- Building societies and construction companies criticise plans to raise taxes in their sector.
- European Commission approves German regional aid plans for next three years.
DIE WELT
- Parliamentary president Rita Suessmuth inisists she only used government flights for trips involved with her work.
- Stock experts expect car companies to be among the winners in the share markets of 1997.
- Hamburg-based HWWA Institute says unemployment will only fall when state cuts taxes, puts finances in order and cuts social security payments.
